summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount. Holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount, which confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias — 4/6 judged more than 2/3 'because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces'
Different numbers must mean different amounts (denies equivalence)
Makes 'equivalents' by ADDING the same number to top and bottom (2/3 → 3/4)
Compares shaded amounts across different-sized wholes
Thinks changing only the numerator or only the denominator keeps the value

activities.title: Split each part of a fixed bar (2/3 becomes 4/6)
steps: Shade two of three equal parts of a bar to show 2/3.
Split every third into two equal pieces by drawing a line through each part; count that four of six parts are now shaded and write 4/6.
Describe what happened to the length of shaded strip: it did not grow or shrink, there are just more lines.
Keep splitting to generate the family: split each part into three for 6/9, into four for 8/12; each time check the shaded strip stays the same length.

Test changing only one number: on an identical bar change only the bottom number (2/3 to 2/6) or only the top number (2/3 to 3/3) and shade it; check that the shaded amount changes, so changing just one part does NOT make an equivalent fraction.
Try the trap: add one to the top and one to the bottom (2/3 to 3/4) and shade 3/4 of an identical bar; compare the shaded length with the original 2/3.
activities.insight: Splitting each part (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) makes more, smaller pieces that cover exactly the same amount; for fractions like 2/3, changing only one of the two numbers, or adding one to each, shifts the amount, so neither is a way to make an equivalent fraction.

activities.title: Fraction wall: which rows line up
steps: Use a fraction wall of stacked equal-length rows (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, ninths) and find where rows end at the same vertical line.
Identify equivalents by alignment: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6, and 2/3 = 4/6.
Explain in words why two fractions that reach the same line are equal (they cover the same length of the identical whole).
Check a non-example: does 2/3 line up with 3/4? Note it does not, so they are not equivalent.
activities.insight: A fraction wall is a reliable reference: fractions that cover the same length of the identical whole name the same amount, regardless of how many pieces.

activities.title: Same point on the number line
steps: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and mark thirds above it (1/3, 2/3).
On the same line, mark sixths below it (1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6, including 4/6 against 2/3).
Place 2/3 and 4/6 and check whether they land on the same point or different points.
Repeat with 1/2 and 2/4 (marking halves and quarters) to confirm they coincide.
activities.insight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude and land on the same point of a number line, independent of how the line is partitioned.

activities.title: Sort, match and complete equivalents
steps: Match pairs of equivalent fractions (for example 1/2 with 2/4, 2/3 with 4/6), justifying each with a quick diagram.
Complete the missing value: 2/3 = __/6, and explain how the splitting gives the answer.
Sort a set into 'equivalent to 2/3' and 'not equivalent', deliberately including the additive trap 3/4, and explain why 3/4 does not belong.
When comparing shaded amounts, always use identical-sized wholes, never different-sized wholes.
activities.insight: Identifying and completing equivalents consolidates the idea; the additive trap, together with a required explanation, checks whether the child multiplies both parts rather than adding.

activities.title: Predict, overlay, explain (diagnostic)
steps: Look at two identical bars held apart: one shaded 2/3, one shaded 4/6.
Predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME as 2/3, and state a reason BEFORE checking.
Slide the second bar onto the first and observe whether the shaded regions coincide.
Respond to a claim: 'Mia says 4/6 is more because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces.' Explain why she is wrong.
Generate one further fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram and justify it.
activities.insight: The stated reason, not just the final answer, reveals whether the child holds the whole constant and compares the shaded amount, or falls into whole-number or additive thinking.

checkQuestion: Here are two identical chocolate bars. The first is split into three equal parts with two of them shaded (2/3). The second is split into six equal parts with four of them shaded (4/6). Mia says 4/6 is more chocolate, because 4 is more than 2 and there are more pieces. Is she right? How much of each bar is shaded, and WHY are they the same or different?
checkAnswer: They are equal — 2/3 = 4/6. The same amount of chocolate is shaded on both bars; the second bar just has each third split into two, so four smaller sixths cover exactly the same length as two thirds. Mia is wrong: more pieces are each smaller, so the total amount is the same.
